title: Retry with backoff in fetch_page
tldr: `fetch_page` now retries HTTP 429 and 503 up to four attempts with exponential backoff, and honors `Retry-After` up to an 8 second cap. Other failures still raise immediately, and `FetchError` now reports how many attempts were made. Tests pin the wait sequence by injecting a fake `sleep`.
assumptions: This is a small invented sample repository used for the demo. I ran its 6 tests and all passed.

body: `fetch_page(url, session)` sends one HTTP GET through a `session` object and returns the body on status 200. Before this change, any other status raised `FetchError` immediately.

HTTP 429 means the server is rate limiting the caller. HTTP 503 means it is temporarily unavailable. Both usually clear within seconds. A server can send a `Retry-After` header to say how long to wait.
full: **Mental model.** A session is any object with `get(url)` that returns something with `status`, `body`, and `headers`. Tests use a small fake, so no network is involved.

what.text: `fetch_page` retries HTTP 429 and 503 up to 4 attempts with waits of 0.5s, 1s, and 2s. It honors `Retry-After`. Other non-200 statuses still fail fast.
what.label: stated

why.text: Pages fail intermittently at peak load, and the whole job aborts on the first failure.
why.label: stated

decisions.text: `Retry-After` is capped at 8 seconds so one slow server cannot stall a worker.
decisions.label: stated

decisions.text: The wait goes through an injectable `sleep` argument, so tests run without real delays.
decisions.label: inferred

reasons: new retry loop in the request path
changes how failures surface to callers
wait computation honors a server header, capped at 8 seconds

items.why: the cap is the only guard against a stalled worker

items.try: four 503 responses in a row, then a 200
items.why: the attempt limit decides whether the fourth answer is used
non-retryable statuses must still fail on the first attempt

controls.title: Calls to external services
controls.requirement: The vendor is in the vendor register. Every request has a timeout. Retries are bounded in count and total wait, and honor the vendor's rate limit headers.
controls.failure: An unbounded retry or wait, a request with no timeout, or a vendor outside the register.
controls.evidence: Attempts stop at `max_attempts=4` and each wait is capped at 8 seconds, from the code. No timeout argument appears in the diff; the `session` object is supplied by the caller. The vendor register is not in this repository.
controls.signoff: Reviewer; procurement for a new vendor.

controls.title: Change management
controls.requirement: The PR states how the change is undone (flag, clean revert, or a rollback plan) and links the ticket.
controls.failure: Production code changes with no stated way to undo it.
controls.evidence: How to undo above reads Clean revert. No ticket key in the branch name or commit message.

body: The toy request is `https://example.com/report`. The server answers 503 twice, then 200. Pick another case to see the other paths: a long `Retry-After`, retries running out, and a status that is never retried.

groups.title: Decide what counts as transient
body: [[s_retryable]] names the two statuses worth retrying. [[s_error]] adds an `attempts` field to `FetchError` so callers can log how hard the function tried. It defaults to 1, which keeps existing `FetchError(message)` calls valid.

groups.title: Compute the wait
body: [[s_delay]] returns `Retry-After` when the server supplies it, limited to `max_delay`. Otherwise the wait doubles from 0.5s and stops growing at 8s. `attempt` counts from 1, so the first wait equals `base`.

groups.title: The retry loop
body: [[s_loop]] returns on 200 and raises immediately for statuses outside `RETRYABLE`. On the final attempt it raises instead of sleeping, so no time is wasted after the last failure. Otherwise it sleeps and tries again. `sleep` is an argument, defaulting to `time.sleep`.

groups.title: Tests pin the waits
body: [[s_test_cap]] and [[s_test_giveup]] pass `waits.append` as `sleep`, so they assert the exact wait sequence without delaying the run.

full.callout: `Retry-After` may also be an HTTP date. The loop calls `float()` on the header, and `float("Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT")` raises `ValueError` when run. This is observed behavior of the code, not a stated goal of the change.
full.title: Edge case not covered

Sleep 8.0s, then send the request again.

Status 200: return the body.
Attempt 1: the server answers 503.

waits.title: Wait after each failed attempt
waits.caption: Without a Retry-After header, from running backoff_delay for attempts 1 to 6. The wait doubles, then stops at the 8 second cap.

quiz.prompt: Why does backoff_delay limit a server's Retry-After value to max_delay?
options: The HTTP specification does not allow Retry-After values above 8 seconds.
A server could ask for a very long wait, so the cap bounds each attempt's stall.
Retry-After arrives in milliseconds, so the cap converts it to a usable range.
The cap makes the retry loop stop early, before it can reach max_attempts.
quiz.explain: The cap bounds the worst case wait per attempt. In the 30 second case the function waits 8.0 seconds.

quiz.prompt: The server answers 503 on all four attempts. What happens?
options: Four waits happen, then FetchError is raised after the fourth attempt.
The function gives up quietly and returns None after the fourth attempt.
FetchError is raised after the third attempt, with attempts equal to 3.
Three waits of 0.5s, 1.0s, and 2.0s happen, then FetchError has attempts=4.
quiz.explain: The loop raises on the last attempt instead of sleeping, so there are three waits for four attempts. This is the 503 on every attempt case in the stepper.

quiz.prompt: The server answers 404 on the first request. What does fetch_page do?
options: It raises FetchError(attempts=1) immediately, without any wait.
It retries up to four times, because any failure may be transient.
It waits 0.5s once, then raises FetchError on the second try.
It returns the response body so the caller can inspect the status.
quiz.explain: 404 is outside RETRYABLE, so the loop raises on the first attempt. The test for a 500 asserts one call and attempts equal to 1.

quiz.prompt: What does the sleep argument of fetch_page make possible?
options: Callers can disable retries by passing None.
The retry loop can run on several threads at once.
Tests can record the waits and skip real delays.
The wait can switch from seconds to milliseconds.
quiz.explain: The tests pass waits.append as sleep, so they assert the exact wait sequence and finish instantly.

quiz.prompt: With no Retry-After header, what wait does backoff_delay(6) return?
options: 16.0 seconds, because the doubling keeps going.
8.0 seconds, because 16.0 is limited to max_delay.
4.0 seconds, because the sequence resets after five attempts.
0.5 seconds, because base applies to every attempt.
quiz.explain: The uncapped value would be 0.5 * 2**5 = 16.0. The cap limits it to 8.0. The test for growth asserts 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 8.0.
